name: Myers-Perry Rotating Black Hole
description: The rotating black hole in $D > 4$ spacetime dimensions, the vacuum solution Robert Myers and Malcolm Perry found in 1985, with a separate spin in each independent plane of rotation. In five dimensions it shares its mass and spin with black rings, and from six dimensions up a black hole turning in one plane keeps its horizon at every spin.
convention: The mass $M$ and the angular momentum $J_i$ of each plane fix the mass parameter and the spin parameters through $\mu = 16\pi GM/\left((D-2)\,\Omega_{D-2}\,c^2\right)$ and $a_i = (D-2)J_i/(2Mc)$, with $G$ Newton's constant in $D$ spacetime dimensions and $\Omega_{D-2}$ the area of the unit sphere of $D - 2$ dimensions. A positive spin parameter is rotation toward increasing angle, and we keep factors of $c$ explicit.
history: A wheel in three dimensions of space turns about an axis, and in four the axis is gone: a rotation turns one plane and leaves the plane across it alone, so two wheels can turn at once in two planes that meet at a single point [myers2011]. How does a black hole spin in a space like that? Robert Myers met the question as a doctoral student, when he and his supervisor, Malcolm Perry, were led to black holes in higher dimensions in part by the "renewed excitement in superstring theory" of 1984 [myers2011]. In 1985 they had the answer, a rotating black hole for every dimension $D > 4$: a vacuum solution with a mass and a separate spin for each independent plane of rotation, two planes in five and six dimensions and three in seven [myers1986, myers2011].¶The way in was a trick of Roy Kerr's: his rotating black hole of 1963 can be written as flat spacetime plus the square of a single null vector, the Kerr-Schild form, which Roberto Emparan and Harvey Reall call "a sort of linearization of the problem" [kerr1963, emparan2008]. Myers and Perry looked for black holes of that form in more dimensions, and Myers credits the form with letting them derive the solutions [myers2011]. With a single spin $a$ in $D$ dimensions their metric is $$ds^2 = -c^2dt^2 + \frac{\mu}{r^{D-5}\Sigma}\left(c\,dt - a\sin^2\theta\,d\phi\right)^2 + \frac{\Sigma}{\Delta}dr^2 + \Sigma\,d\theta^2 + \left(r^2 + a^2\right)\sin^2\theta\,d\phi^2 + r^2\cos^2\theta\,d\Omega_{D-4}^2,$$ with $\Sigma = r^2 + a^2\cos^2\theta$ and $\Delta = r^2 + a^2 - \mu/r^{D-5}$ [emparan2008]. At $D = 4$ it is Kerr's metric in the coordinates of Boyer and Lindquist, and with $a = 0$ it is Frank Tangherlini's static black hole of 1963 [emparan2008, myers2011, tangherlini1963]. Coordinates like Eddington's, which ride in on the infalling light rays, carry the metric through the horizon [myers2011].¶Can such a hole spin as fast as it likes? Kerr's cannot: its angular momentum is held to $J \le GM^2/c$, and past that the horizon is gone and the singularity is naked [emparan2003, emparan2008]. In five dimensions a hole turning in one plane keeps its horizon, at $r_+ = \sqrt{\mu - a^2}$, only while $a^2 < \mu$ [emparan2008]. Inside it there is no second horizon: the Penrose diagram is Schwarzschild's, and the Kretschmann scalar $24\mu^2\left(4r^2 - 3\Sigma\right)\left(4r^2 - \Sigma\right)/\Sigma^6$ diverges on the ring $r = 0$, $\theta = \pi/2$ [myers2011]. From six dimensions up Myers and Perry found no limit: "black holes with a fixed mass may have arbitrarily large angular momentum" [myers1986]. Gravity's pull falls off faster with every dimension added, and the centrifugal barrier keeps its form, "since rotations always refer to motions in a plane": the two meet in $\Delta/r^2 - 1 = -\mu/r^{D-3} + a^2/r^2$ [emparan2008].¶What does a hole spinning that fast look like? A "pancake", in the word of Emparan and Myers, whose reckoning of 2003 has the horizon spread out in the plane of rotation, about as wide as $a$, and shrink in every direction across that plane [emparan2003]. A pancake thin enough is a black membrane to anyone standing on it, and Ruth Gregory and Raymond Laflamme's instability of 1993 then takes over: a black membrane ripples along its length and breaks up [emparan2003, gregorylaflamme1993]. So Emparan and Myers argued that the fastest holes are unstable, and that gravity in higher dimensions holds a spinning black hole to a bound of Kerr's kind after all, "through a dynamical decay mechanism" [emparan2003]. The onset of the instability turned up in the numerical work of Óscar Dias, Pau Figueras, Ricardo Monteiro, Jorge Santos, and Emparan in 2009, at the spin where the second derivative of the entropy with respect to the angular momentum vanishes [dias2009]. Followed on a computer in six dimensions by Figueras, Markus Kunesch, Luis Lehner, and Saran Tunyasuvunakool, the pancake breaks into "a sequence of concentric rings connected by segments of black membrane on the rotation plane", and the membranes thin away to a naked singularity [figueras2017].¶Do mass and spin still fix the black hole, as they fix Kerr's in four dimensions [emparan2002]? Five dimensions hold a second kind of black hole, the rotating black ring of Emparan and Reall, whose horizon is a circle times a 2-sphere and whose rotation balances its own gravity [emparan2002]. For a range of mass and angular momentum two black rings and a Myers-Perry black hole exist with the same values of both [emparan2002]. With one more assumption the hole gets its uniqueness back: Yoshiyuki Morisawa and Daisuke Ida proved in 2004 that a black hole of five dimensions with a spherical horizon and two commuting rotational symmetries is "uniquely characterized by the mass, and a pair of the angular momenta" [morisawa2004]. Even that hole is unstable when it turns fast enough: in the simulations of Masaru Shibata and Hirotaka Yoshino a hole with one spin above about $a = 0.87\sqrt{\mu}$ deforms into a bar [shibata2010].¶Does Kerr's hidden symmetry survive the move to more dimensions, the extra constant of motion that makes its geodesic equation integrable [emparan2008]? In five dimensions it does: Valeri Frolov and Dejan Stojković found a Killing tensor beside the hole's three Killing vectors in 2003, and proved along the way that no circular orbit in a plane of rotation is stable [frolov2003]. By 2007 Frolov and David Kubizňák had it in every dimension and for every set of spins, and Don Page, Kubizňák, Muraari Vasudevan, and Pavel Krtouš had shown that the motion of a free particle is completely integrable [frolov2007, page2007]. Set the two spins of the hole of five dimensions equal and the symmetry grows again: the metric depends on the radius alone, and each surface around the hole is a 3-sphere with a homogeneous metric, squashed along its Hopf circles [myers2011, emparan2008]. That symmetry let Keiju Murata and Jiro Soda reduce the perturbations of the hole to master equations in 2008 and prove it stable under them [murata2008].

related.text: The case $D = 4$, where there is one plane to turn in and the spin cannot pass $a = GM/c^2$ [myers1986].
Every spin switched off. The horizon is a round sphere again, of radius $\mu^{1/(D-3)}$ [myers2011].

Another vacuum solution of five dimensions built on squashed 3-spheres. With equal spins this black hole stretches its Hopf circles, and the monopole shrinks its own to a point at the centre [grossperry1983, emparan2008].
